stories.name: McKenzie Coan
stories.hook: Paralympic swimmer, world record holder — the same condition as Unbreakable's founder.
stories.featuredHook: Doctors never expected her to stand. Today she's a world record holder in Paralympic swimming.

stories.name: Mimie Mathy
stories.hook: More than 40 years in show business, Legion of Honour — an icon of French television.

stories.name: Raul Krauthausen
stories.hook: From living inaccessibility to social entrepreneurship — Order of Merit of Germany.

stories.name: Stephen Hawking
stories.hook: More than 50 years with the disease, one of the most remarkable scientific careers of the century.

stories.name: Tionne Watkins
stories.hook: Singer of the group TLC, an active advocate in the fight against sickle cell disease.

stories.name: Katie Ledecky
stories.hook: The most decorated female swimmer in Olympic history — despite a POTS diagnosis in 2015.

stories.name: Gaelynn Lea
stories.hook: Violinist, winner of NPR's Tiny Desk Contest — against thousands of able-bodied contestants.

stories.name: Emilio Gavira
stories.hook: Actor and baritone, Goya-nominated — a dual career spanning film and opera.

stories.name: Martín Caparrós
stories.hook: Renowned Argentine writer and journalist, still working through the diagnosis.

stories.name: Álvaro Valera
stories.hook: 7 Paralympic Games, gold in Sydney 2000, now an entrepreneur — a path that mirrors the founder's own.

stories.name: Shane Burcaw
stories.hook: Writer and content creator, over 760 million views for a life told without filter or pity.

stories.name: Marta Arce
stories.hook: Paralympic judoka, flag bearer for the Spanish delegation and bronze medalist at the Paris 2024 Games.

stories.name: Jessica Long
stories.hook: Six Paralympic Games, 18 titles, 31 medals in total — one of the most decorated swimmers in Paralympic history.

stories.name: Tatyana McFadden
stories.hook: The only athlete in history, able-bodied or not, to win all four major marathons in the same year.

stories.name: Marla Runyan
stories.hook: First legally blind athlete to compete at the Olympics, 8th in the 1500m at Sydney 2000 against sighted runners.

stories.name: Anthony Robles
stories.hook: Undefeated NCAA wrestling champion on one leg (36 wins, 0 losses) — Most Outstanding Wrestler of the tournament.

stories.name: Zion Clark
stories.hook: Guinness World Record holder for the hand-sprint, college wrestler turned professional MMA fighter.

stories.name: Flo Hyman
stories.hook: Olympic silver medal in volleyball 1984 — a national award for women's sport now bears her name.

stories.name: Erik Weihenmayer
stories.hook: First blind person to summit Everest and complete the Seven Summits — now a speaker and entrepreneur.

stories.name: Itzhak Perlman
stories.hook: Paralyzed in the legs by polio at age 4, he has performed seated for more than 60 years — 15 Grammy Awards, Kennedy Center Honors.

stories.name: Nick Vujicic
stories.hook: Born without arms or legs, he became an international speaker and entrepreneur, founder of Life Without Limbs.

stories.name: Aimee Mullins
stories.hook: Both legs amputated before her first birthday, a pioneer of Paralympic sprinting at Atlanta 1996 — later a model and actress.

stories.name: Sam Berns
stories.hook: Living with progeria, he delivered a TEDx talk at 17 — viewed more than 54 million times — on his philosophy of happiness.

stories.name: Sia
stories.hook: Publicly revealed she lives with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, without ever pausing an international career as a singer and producer.

stories.name: Jean-Dominique Bauby
stories.hook: Editor-in-chief of Elle, struck by locked-in syndrome after a stroke, he wrote an entire book by blinking his left eye.

stories.name: Stephen Wiltshire
stories.hook: Diagnosed autistic at age 3, he draws entire cityscapes from memory after a single flyover — awarded an MBE for his art.

stories.name: Christy Brown
stories.hook: Paralyzed from birth, only his left foot obeyed him — he made it his tool for writing and painting. His autobiography inspired My Left Foot, winner of two Academy Awards.

stories.name: Charles Mingus
stories.hook: Struck by ALS in 1977, he kept composing until his death, humming his last melodies into a tape recorder — a towering figure of 20th-century jazz, his archives acquired by the U.S. Library of Congress.

stories.name: Michael J. Fox
stories.hook: Diagnosed with early-onset Parkinson's disease at the edge of his thirties, hidden for seven years before going public in 1998 — his foundation has become the world's largest private funder of Parkinson's research, with close to two billion dollars raised to date.

stories.name: Andrea Bocelli
stories.hook: Impaired by congenital glaucoma from birth, then rendered completely blind at 12 by a football struck full in the face during a match — more than 90 million records sold, duets with Pavarotti and Céline Dion, opening performance at the 2006 World Cup.

stories.name: Stevie Wonder
stories.hook: Blinded at six weeks after a premature birth, he scored his first Billboard No. 1 at 13 — 25 Grammy Awards, the only artist to win Album of the Year three times in a row, Kennedy Center Honors, Presidential Medal of Freedom.

stories.name: Joni Mitchell
stories.hook: Paralyzed by polio at nine, she learned to walk again — then turned the lasting weakness in her left hand into a language of nearly fifty guitar tunings that changed popular song: eleven Grammy Awards, Kennedy Center Honors, induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

stories.name: Neil Young
stories.hook: Partially paralyzed by polio at 5, then struck by seizures from the earliest days of his career as a musician, he has built a career spanning more than sixty years and still going — twice inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Officer of the Order of Canada, nicknamed the “Godfather of Grunge.”

stories.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
stories.hook: Deaf by the end of his twenties, he composed and conducted the premiere of his 9th Symphony in 1824 without being able to hear the audience's ovation — one of the most performed works in the history of Western music.

stories.name: Temple Grandin
stories.hook: Diagnosed at two with a supposed “brain injury” — the only term 1950s American medicine had to offer — she became a professor at Colorado State University: nearly half of the cattle handled in North America now passes through facilities she designed.

stories.name: Daniel Tammet
stories.hook: Diagnosed with Asperger's and synesthesia at 25, he recited the first 22,514 digits of pi from memory in just over five hours, seated in front of Einstein's blackboard at Oxford — then learned Icelandic in a week for television, before writing a worldwide bestseller translated into some twenty languages.

stories.name: John Nash
stories.hook: Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia at 30, forcibly hospitalized several times over more than a decade, he returned to research and received, 44 years after his thesis, the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics — then the Abel Prize in 2015, days before his death.

stories.name: Annette Funicello
stories.hook: Diagnosed with multiple sclerosis at 44, she kept the illness private for five years before revealing it publicly in 1992, partly to silence press rumors that she was drunk in public — former star Mouseketeer for Disney, icon of the beach party movies, founder of a research fund that still bears her name.

stories.name: Wilma Rudolph
stories.hook: Struck by polio at 5, she wore a leg brace until about eleven or twelve, with doctors doubting she would ever walk normally again — she became a sprinter and won three gold medals at the 1960 Rome Olympics, a first for an American woman in track and field at a single Olympiad.

stories.name: Richard Branson
stories.hook: Dyslexic and written off as a poor student by his teachers in 1960s England, he left school at sixteen — now founder of the Virgin Group and a billionaire, he flew to space himself in 2021, aboard a vessel built by his own company.

stories.name: Bebe Vio
stories.hook: All four limbs amputated after fulminant meningitis at 11, she became the first fencer in the world to compete with all four prosthetic limbs — two individual foil Paralympic titles (Rio 2016, Tokyo 2020), multiple world and European titles.

stories.name: Marie Bochet
stories.hook: Born with agenesis of the left forearm, she put on her first skis at five — 8 Paralympic gold medals, 22 world titles in para alpine skiing, before becoming chef de mission of the French delegation at the Milan-Cortina 2026 Games.

stories.name: Judith Scott
stories.hook: Born with Down syndrome and left deaf by an undiagnosed childhood case of scarlet fever, she spent thirty-five years institutionalized without learning a single word of language — before becoming, from age 44, a fiber sculptor exhibited at MoMA, the Brooklyn Museum, and the 2017 Venice Biennale.

stories.name: Geerat J. Vermeij
stories.hook: Blind since age three, he built his career as a paleobiologist by touch alone — MacArthur Fellowship 1992, Daniel Giraud Elliot Medal 2000, elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2022.

stories.name: Chris Nikic
stories.hook: Living with Down syndrome, he completed the first full Ironman ever finished by a man with this condition in 2020, 14 minutes before the cutoff — a record certified by Guinness World Records — then did it again in Kona in 2022, on his 23rd birthday.

stories.name: Sarah Storey
stories.pathologyLabel: Congenital absence of a functional left hand
stories.hook: Born without a functional left hand after the umbilical cord wrapped around it in utero, she became the most decorated British Paralympian in history across all sports — 30 Paralympic medals including 19 gold, across 9 Games between 1992 and 2024, first in swimming then on the bike.

stories.name: Oksana Masters
stories.hook: Born in Ukraine with bilateral tibial hemimelia, given up to an orphanage then adopted by an American woman at 7, she became the most decorated Winter Paralympian in Team USA history — 24 Paralympic medals across four sports.

stories.name: Ntando Mahlangu
stories.hook: Both legs amputated below the knee at ten after congenital bilateral fibular hemimelia, he became Paralympic champion and world record holder in the long jump and 200m at Tokyo 2020 — before a road accident kept him out of Paris 2024.

stories.name: David Paterson
stories.hook: Legally blind since he was three months old, he became the 55th Governor of the State of New York overnight — without ever having been elected to the office by voters.

stories.name: Terry Pratchett
stories.hook: Diagnosed at 59 with a rare, early-onset form of Alzheimer's, the author of Discworld kept writing bestseller after bestseller for eight years, between dictation software and a public fight for dementia research and the right to choose his own death.

stories.name: Wolfgang Schäuble
stories.hook: Three bullets in the back in the middle of a campaign rally. Twenty-seven years later, he presided over the Bundestag from his wheelchair.

stories.name: Yasuhiko Funago
stories.hook: Paralyzed by ALS, he now communicates only with his eyes — and became one of the first two severely disabled lawmakers in the history of Japan's parliament.

stories.name: Eiko Kimura
stories.hook: Quadriplegic since the age of eight months, she had seats removed from Japan's parliament so that her wheelchair could get in.

stories.name: Jordon Steele-John
stories.hook: Cerebral palsy from birth, the youngest senator in Australian history at 23 — and a voice for victims of abuse in institutional care.

stories.name: Karine Elharrar
stories.hook: Israel's energy minister, she was denied entry to COP26 for lack of a ramp for her wheelchair.

stories.name: Michael Masutha
stories.hook: Blind from birth in apartheid South Africa, he became the country's Minister of Justice.

stories.name: Gilberto Rincón Gallardo
stories.hook: Shortened arms from birth, imprisoned thirty-two times for his political battles — he became the first president of Mexico's anti-discrimination authority.

stories.name: Helga Stevens
stories.hook: Born deaf, she became Belgium's first deaf lawyer, then a candidate for President of the European Parliament.

stories.name: Ádám Kósa
stories.hook: The first deaf member in the history of the European Parliament, he served there for fifteen years, in sign language.

stories.name: Mara Gabrilli
stories.hook: A model left quadriplegic by a car accident, she wrote the law that changed the lives of 45 million Brazilians with disabilities.

stories.name: Golda Meir
stories.hook: Prime Minister of Israel, she hid the cancer eating away at her for thirteen years — even leading the Yom Kippur War with that secret.

stories.name: Georges Pompidou
stories.hook: President of France, he hid his illness to the grave: the first bulletin on his state of health was not published until six days after his death.

stories.name: John Paul II
stories.hook: Twenty-seven years as pope, including more than a decade of Parkinson's on display to the whole world — right up to that final appearance when he could no longer utter a word.

stories.name: Kim Dae-jung
stories.pathologyLabel: Permanent injuries from an assassination attempt (hip and leg)
stories.hook: A truck that left him disabled, an abduction on the high seas: survivor of two attempts on his life, he became president and received the Nobel Peace Prize.

stories.name: Chandrika Kumaratunga
stories.hook: A suicide bombing cost her an eye three days before the election. She was re-elected President of Sri Lanka and called on her country to stay calm from her hospital bed.

stories.name: Václav Havel
stories.hook: A former dissident jailed by the communist regime, he governed for thirteen years while facing lung cancer, its recurrence, then emergency surgery — without ever leaving office.

stories.name: Tony Coelho
stories.hook: Epilepsy diagnosed in seminary barred him from the priesthood. He became the third-ranking figure in the U.S. Congress and the author of America's landmark disability law.

stories.name: Talleyrand
stories.hook: A clubfoot from childhood, stripped of his birthright as the eldest son, he became one of the most influential diplomats in the history of Europe, serving five successive regimes.

stories.name: Dilma Rousseff
stories.hook: Tortured for twenty-two days under the military dictatorship, then cancer fought while in power: she became the first woman president of Brazil.

stories.name: Lenín Moreno
stories.hook: A bullet in the back left him paraplegic. Twenty years later, he became the only head of state in the world governing from a wheelchair.

stories.name: Hussein of Jordan
stories.hook: Dying of cancer, he signed his last act as king from his bed: changing the line of succession, fourteen days before his death, after forty-seven years on the throne.

stories.name: Natalia Partyka
stories.pathologyLabel: Congenital malformation (agenesis of the right hand and forearm)
stories.hook: Born without a right hand or forearm, she became the only table tennis player to compete in both the Olympic and Paralympic Games, with four consecutive titles to her name.

stories.name: Olga Skorokhodova
stories.hook: Deaf and blind since the age of five, she became the first researcher in the world to make her own perception of the world the very subject of her science.

stories.name: Fatma Omar
stories.hook: Polio at age one, four consecutive Paralympic powerlifting titles and one last world podium past the age of 48.

stories.name: Henry Wanyoike
stories.hook: Blinded overnight at 20 after a stroke, he became Paralympic 5000m champion, linked to his guide by a simple cord tied to his hand.

stories.name: Satoshi Fukushima
stories.hook: Deafblind from the age of 18, he became the first deafblind professor in the history of the University of Tokyo, teaching through braille tapped onto his fingers.

stories.name: Cheah Liek Hou
stories.hook: A nerve damaged at birth left him with a weak right hand. He became the very first Paralympic champion in the history of para-badminton.

stories.name: Song Lingling
stories.hook: Her legs paralyzed by polio, she entered a swimming pool for the first time at thirteen — seven years later, she was Paralympic champion and held the world record.

stories.name: Deepa Malik
stories.hook: Paralyzed at 29 by a spinal tumor, she became the first Indian woman to win a Paralympic medal, across all sports.

stories.name: Mark Malyar
stories.hook: Enrolled in swimming at five to rehabilitate his cerebral palsy, he now holds four swimming world records simultaneously.

stories.name: Hellen Saohaga
stories.hook: Born with a malformation of the legs in an archipelago with no adaptive sports structure whatsoever, she became the first Paralympic athlete in the history of the Solomon Islands.

stories.name: Yip Pin Xiu
stories.hook: Diagnosed with a genetic neuromuscular disease, she became Singapore's first Paralympic champion — and the youngest Nominated Member of Parliament in the country's history.

stories.name: Mayumi Narita
stories.hook: Her legs paralyzed at thirteen by transverse myelitis, she became Japan's “Queen of the Water”: fifteen titles and six Paralympic Games, from 1996 to 2021.

stories.name: Farida Bedwei
stories.hook: Diagnosed with cerebral palsy at one and homeschooled for lack of suitable schools, she became a principal engineer at Microsoft after co-founding a company that digitized microfinance in Ghana.

stories.name: Zakia Khudadadi
stories.pathologyLabel: Congenital malformation of the left arm
stories.hook: Evacuated from Kabul as the Taliban were taking the city, this Afghan woman born with an impaired arm won the very first medal in the history of the Refugee Paralympic Team.

stories.name: Daniel Dias
stories.pathologyLabel: Congenital malformation of all four limbs
stories.hook: Born with a congenital malformation affecting all four limbs, he became the most decorated male Paralympic swimmer in history, with twenty-seven medals across four Games.

stories.name: Wanda Díaz-Merced
stories.hook: Blinded in her early twenties by diabetes, this astrophysicist invented a method to “listen” to the stars, now used by astronomers around the world.

stories.name: Kurt Fearnley
stories.hook: Born with sacral agenesis that raised fears he would not survive his first week, he became a three-time Paralympic champion — then crawled 96 km through the jungle to raise awareness of men's health.

stories.name: Ellie Cole
stories.hook: One leg amputated at two because of a rare tumor, she became the most decorated female Paralympian in Australian history, with seventeen medals across four Games.

stories.name: Zanele Situ
stories.hook: Paralyzed at twelve by spinal tuberculosis under apartheid, she became the first Black South African woman to become Paralympic champion, in Sydney in 2000.

stories.name: Charl du Toit
stories.hook: Cerebral palsy affecting one whole side of his body, spotted by chance at a physiotherapist's at seventeen: he became a double Paralympic sprint champion in Rio, breaking two world records.

stories.name: Alan Oliveira
stories.hook: Both legs amputated at three weeks old to save his life, he dethroned Oscar Pistorius in the 200 meters at London 2012 — seven hundredths of a second that made news around the world.

stories.name: Lee Thiam Wah
stories.hook: His legs paralyzed by polio at eight months, with only six years of schooling for lack of money: he became the Malaysian billionaire at the head of the country's largest convenience store chain, more than 3,000 stores.

stories.name: Srikanth Bolla
stories.hook: Blind from birth, he had to win a lawsuit for the right to study science in high school — the first blind international student at MIT, he became a social entrepreneur carried all the way to the screen by a hit biopic.

stories.name: Amit Goffer
stories.hook: Quadriplegic after an ATV accident with his family, this engineer invented the ReWalk exoskeleton in seven years — approved in the United States, it has enabled hundreds of paralyzed people to walk again.

stories.name: Cai Lei
stories.hook: A top executive in Chinese e-commerce, diagnosed with ALS at 41: he can no longer walk or speak, yet still runs, through eye movements alone, a platform that has advanced hundreds of treatments.

stories.name: Kjell Inge Røkke
stories.hook: Dyslexic, he left school at 14 to work as a fisherman on Alaskan trawlers — forty years on, he chairs one of Norway's largest industrial groups, at the head of a fortune of more than ten billion dollars.

stories.name: Olivier Jeannel
stories.hook: Deaf since the age of two, unable to make a phone call on his own: he founded the company that now runs France's national relay center, more than 450,000 calls made possible in three years.

stories.name: Collette Divitto
stories.hook: Living with Down syndrome, a graduate turned down by every employer in Boston, she launched her own cookie business from the family kitchen — fifteen employees later, her story inspired a film honored at the Student Academy Awards.

stories.name: Sebenzile Matsebula
stories.hook: Paraplegic after contracting polio at ten months, she first led disability policy in the South African Presidency before becoming co-director and shareholder of a company employing more than 150 people.

stories.name: Masayoshi Son
stories.hook: Diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B at 25 and given three to five years to live, he recovered and took back the reins of SoftBank — becoming one of the most influential technology investors in the world, from Yahoo to Alibaba.

stories.name: Hikari Ōe
stories.hook: He did not speak his first sentence until age six, imitating a bird's song. Having become a composer with perfect pitch, he would inspire the novel that won his father the Nobel Prize in Literature.

stories.name: Yayoi Kusama
stories.hook: Haunted since childhood by hallucinations of polka dots and infinite nets, she made them the substance of one of the most visited bodies of work in contemporary art, without ever ceasing to speak about them openly.

stories.name: Lee Hee-ah
stories.pathologyLabel: Congenital malformation of the hands and legs
stories.hook: With two fingers on each hand and legs amputated in childhood, she became an acclaimed classical pianist, before putting her fame in the service of inter-Korean reconciliation.

stories.name: Tai Lihua
stories.hook: Deaf from the age of two after a medical treatment, she led a troupe of deaf dancers in a routine seen by hundreds of millions of Chinese viewers, timed to vibrations rather than to the music.

stories.name: Ravindra Jain
stories.hook: Blind from birth, he composed the music for the most watched television series in India's history and scored more than a hundred films, without ever seeing a single screen.

stories.name: Sheikh Imam
stories.hook: Blind since his first months of life, he became, alongside the poet Ahmed Fouad Negm, one of Egypt's most popular voices of protest — banned from the official airwaves but sung in chorus across the whole country.

stories.name: Salif Keita
stories.hook: Rejected by his father and his village because of his albinism, he became “the Golden Voice of Africa” and one of the most committed advocates for people with albinism across the continent.

stories.name: Edvard Munch
stories.hook: Haunted by grief and anxiety since childhood, the painter of The Scream went through a severe nervous breakdown documented in his lifetime — an episode he considered inseparable from his art.

stories.name: Cazuza
stories.hook: The first public face of AIDS in Brazil, this rock lyricist revealed he was HIV-positive in the middle of an interview, in 1989, helping to change how an entire country looked at the disease.

stories.name: Vaslav Nijinsky
stories.hook: The most famous dancer of his time, he saw his career come to an abrupt halt at thirty, struck down by schizophrenia — a diagnosis exceptionally well documented by the greatest psychiatrists of the era.
